prompt: What was the main finding of the Hawthorne experiments?

options.text: Productivity rose whatever working condition was changed, because workers felt observed and cared for
Better lighting is the main driver of productivity
Piece rates are the only effective incentive
Formal rules matter more than the informal organisation

explanation: Social factors – attention, group morale, informal norms – explained the results.

prompt: Which informal rules did the Hawthorne work group set up?

options.text: Do not produce too much
Do not produce too little
Never tell a superior anything that may harm a group member
Always report colleagues who slack

explanation: Plus: members with a slightly higher status should not play the boss.

Exit
Voice

prompt: Which are examples of intrinsic motivation?

options.text: The pleasure of solving a hard problem
A sense of accomplishment
Finding the work meaningful

prompt: Which statements about the psychological contract are correct?

options.text: Retributions and contributions can be immaterial
The subjective perception matters more than the objective value

statement: The Hawthorne experiments confirmed the scientific-management prediction that better physical conditions raise productivity.
explanation: Productivity rose even when conditions got worse – social factors explained it.

statement: In the Hawthorne studies, the informal organisation turned out to matter more than the formal organisation.
explanation: Group morale and informal leaders strongly shaped productivity.

statement: For March & Simon, what matters is the objective, monetary value of contributions and retributions.
explanation: It is the subjective, sometimes symbolic perception of the members.

statement: In Hirschman's model, exit requires an external labour market to be available.
explanation: People leave silently when they have alternatives.

statement: Etzioni argues that organisations use only one incentive mechanism at a time.
explanation: They combine coercion, remuneration and identification in variable proportions.

statement: Introducing a fine for late parents at a daycare can increase lateness because it turns a moral obligation into a price.
explanation: Extrinsic incentives can crowd out intrinsic motivation.

statement: Voice means staying in the organisation and protesting in the hope of change.
explanation: Exit = leave silently; exit & voice = leave and complain; loyalty = stay and accept.

prompt: Apply March & Simon's contribution–retribution model to Google. Is the equilibrium achieved?
modelAnswer:
March & Simon: people stay as long as perceived retributions ≥ contributions.
Retributions at Google: high pay and stock, prestige of belonging to an elite, luxurious offices and perks, interesting technical problems, freedom for personal projects, talented colleagues.
Contributions: very heavy workload, availability at night and on holiday, pressure and stress (health and private life), subordination to sometimes unqualified managers, conformity to a dominant profile, accepting bureaucracy (goal reviews).
Missing or weak retributions for many: recognition (“everyone is great”), promotion opportunities (overqualification), meaning and personal impact (“a cog in a giant machine”), voice (dissent not tolerated).
Conclusion: for star engineers the balance is positive; for many others it is fragile or negative. They may restore it by reducing contributions (disengagement) or by exit – a retention risk that the perks alone cannot fix. Remember: perceptions, not objective values, count.

prompt: Present Hirschman's exit–voice–loyalty model and explain what a manager can learn from it.
modelAnswer:
When an organisation no longer matches people's expectations, they react along two axes – stay or leave, keep silent or complain:
• Exit: leave silently (needs an external labour market).
• Exit & voice: leave and voice concerns – may harm the firm's reputation.
• Voice: stay and protest, hoping management will change things.
• Loyalty: stay and accept – out of attachment or out of resignation and lack of resources.
Lessons: silence is not satisfaction (loyalty may hide resignation); voice is valuable information and should be heard before it turns into exit; a firm that suppresses voice gets exits or disengaged “loyal” employees; the reaction depends on alternatives on the labour market and on attachment to the organisation.

prompt: Present Etzioni's three incentive and control mechanisms and give an organisational example for each.
modelAnswer:
Etzioni (1961): organisations use three mechanisms in variable proportions.
• Coercion – coercive power, control and sanctions (stick): prisons, armies, strict monitoring with penalties, “rank and yank”.
• Speculation – remunerative power, compensation and promises (carrot): sales commissions, bonuses, piece rates (Taylor).
• Identification – symbolic or normative power, belonging, vision, values (heart): NGOs, start-ups with a mission, hospitals, companies with strong cultures.
The right mix depends on the work and the people: identification suits professionals and mission-driven organisations; too much coercion or money can crowd out intrinsic motivation.
